Memucan
me-MU-kan
n. (proper, one of the seven princes of Persia and Media)
Persian, of uncertain meaning. He is named three times in Esther 1, as one of the seven princes “which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom” — and his advice set the whole book in motion.

Biblical Definition

The seven counsellors are listed by name: “Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom” (Esther 1:14). When a drunken king asked what should be done with a queen who would not come, Memucan answered, and he answered enormously: “Vashti the queen hath not done wrong to the king only, but also to all the princes, and to all the people that are in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus” (Esther 1:16). He proposed an irrevocable decree deposing her and a letter to every province. And the king took it: “the saying pleased the king and the princes; and the king did according to the word of Memucan” (Esther 1:21). The whole book follows from that counsel — the throne left empty, the search for a new queen, Esther brought in, and a nation saved — none of which Memucan intended.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as one of the seven princes of Persia and Media whose counsel deposed Vashti.

expand to see more

COUNSELLOR, n. Any person who gives advice; particularly, one whose profession is to give advice in law or in affairs of state.

DECREE, n. Judicial decision, or determination of a litigated cause; an edict or law made by a superior as a rule to govern inferiors.

PERSIA, n. A great kingdom of western Asia, which succeeded Babylon in the empire of the East.

MEDIA, n. An ancient country of Asia, joined with Persia in the empire of Cyrus and his successors.

OVERRULE, v.t. To control by superior power or authority; to govern with high authority.

Key Scripture

Esther 1:14 — "And the next unto him was Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom;)"

Esther 1:16 — "And Memucan answered before the king and the princes, Vashti the queen hath not done wrong to the king only, but also to all the princes, and to all the people that are in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus."

Esther 1:21 — "And the saying pleased the king and the princes; and the king did according to the word of Memucan:"

Esther 1:19 — "If it please the king, let there go a royal commandment from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that it be not altered, That Vashti come no more before king Ahasuerus; and let the king give her royal estate unto another that is better than she. Modern Corruption

Policy made in anger and passed in haste is presented as decisive leadership; Memucan's counsel was given to a drunken king, made irrevocable by law, and used by God for the opposite of what he intended.

expand to see more

Esther 1 is a study in how bad government is made. The king is merry with wine, publicly humiliated, and furious; his advisers are at hand; and within a few verses an empire-wide decree has been issued that cannot be reversed, because the law of the Persians and the Medes altereth not. Memucan's speech even inflates the offence — not wrong to the king only, but to all the princes and all the people in all the provinces. Counsel given to flatter a ruler's wounded pride, dressed as concern for the public order, is among the oldest species of political folly, and Scripture puts it on record without comment.

The comment is supplied by what follows. The vacancy Memucan created is the door through which Esther entered, and the God who is never once named in this book governed every step of it. Proverbs says the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will. That is exactly what Esther 1 shows. Men make decrees in anger, and the decrees hold; and the purpose they serve is not the one the counsellor had in mind when he stood up to speak.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Memuwkan (H4462); sar (H8269), a prince; dath (H1881), a decree or law; Achashverowsh (H325), Ahasuerus.

expand to see more

Hebrew Memuwkan (H4462) — Memucan, one of the seven princes of Persia and Media.

Hebrew sar (H8269) — a chief, a prince; the seven who saw the king's face.

Hebrew dath (H1881) — a decree, a law; which altereth not, once written.

Hebrew Achashverowsh (H325) — Ahasuerus, the king whose heart God turned.

Hebrew Vashtiy (H2060) — Vashti, the queen deposed by Memucan's counsel.

Usage

"“Which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom”."

"“The king did according to the word of Memucan” — and the book begins."

"“That it be not altered” — a decree made irrevocable in anger."
